cards.q: What is 'personal data' under GDPR Art. 4(1)?
cards.a: Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (data subject)-directly or indirectly (e.g. name, ID number, location data, online identifier, factors specific to physical/physiological/genetic/mental/economic/cultural/social identity).

figure.caption: Personal data = identifiable person info
figure.shows: Name, email, phone, IP and cookie IDs can qualify.

cards.q: What counts as 'processing' (Art. 4(2))?
cards.a: Any operation (or set of operations) performed on personal data-whether or not by automated means-e.g. collection, recording, organisation, storage, adaptation, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, restriction, erasure or destruction.

figure.caption: Processing covers almost every operation on personal data
figure.shows: Collect, store, use, share, erase - all count as processing under Art. 4(2).

cards.q: Name the core Art. 5 principles for processing personal data.
cards.a: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; accountability.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: List the six lawful bases for processing under GDPR Art. 6(1).
cards.a: Consent; contract; legal obligation; vital interests; public interest / official authority; legitimate interests (controller or third party), with balancing where applicable.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What makes consent valid under GDPR (Art. 4(11) / Art. 7)?
cards.a: Freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication by a clear affirmative action (no pre-ticked boxes). Controller must be able to demonstrate consent; withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What are 'special categories' of personal data (Art. 9)?
cards.a: Data revealing racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religious/philosophical beliefs, trade-union membership; genetic data; biometric data for uniquely identifying a person; health data; data concerning sex life or sexual orientation. Processing is prohibited unless an Art. 9(2) exception applies (e.g. explicit consent).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Controller vs processor - what's the difference?
cards.a: Controller determines purposes and means of processing. Processor processes personal data on behalf of the controller; processing must be governed by a contract/legal act (Art. 28).

figure.caption: Controller decides; processor follows instructions
figure.shows: Controller instructs processor; data subject is the person.

cards.q: Name key data subject rights under GDPR (Ch. III / Art. 12-22).
cards.a: Transparency/information (Art. 12-14); access (Art. 15); rectification (16); erasure/'right to be forgotten' (17); restriction (18); portability (20); object (21); not to be subject solely to automated decisions with legal/similarly significant effects (22). Also withdraw consent and lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is the main takeaway from Lindqvist (C-101/01) for privacy law?
cards.a: Publishing personal data about others on a website can be 'processing' and a transfer of personal data; the household exemption is narrow and does not cover making data accessible on the open internet to an indefinite number of people.

cards.q: What is the household exemption (Art. 2(2)(c))?
cards.a: GDPR does not apply to processing by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity (with no connection to a professional/commercial activity). Narrowly interpreted (see Lindqvist).

figure.caption: Household exemption is narrow
figure.shows: Purely personal/home use only. Publishing to the open internet is usually outside the exemption.

cards.q: When does GDPR apply territorially (Art. 3)?
cards.a: Processing in the context of an establishment of a controller/processor in the Union, regardless of whether processing takes place in the Union; and to non-EU controllers/processors offering goods/services to data subjects in the Union or monitoring their behaviour in the Union.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What does Privacy by Design / Art. 25 require in short?
cards.a: Art. 25(1): implement appropriate technical and organisational measures designed to implement data-protection principles and protect rights (data protection by design), from the earliest stage. Art. 25(2): by default only personal data necessary for each purpose are processed (data protection by default)-short storage, limited accessibility.

figure.alt: Ann Cavoukian Privacy by Design slide
figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: When should you consider a DPIA (Art. 35)?
cards.a: When processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons (especially new technologies / systematic large-scale processing of special categories, systematic monitoring, etc.). Prior consultation with the supervisory authority may be required (Art. 36).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is a key privacy takeaway from Kosinski et al. (PNAS 2013) used in the course readings?
cards.a: Private traits and attributes can be predicted from digital records of human behaviour (e.g. Facebook Likes)-showing how seemingly 'non-sensitive' data can reveal sensitive attributes (function creep / inference risk).

figure.caption: Sensitive inferences
figure.shows: Sensitive inferences

cards.q: What classic phrase did Warren & Brandeis (1890) associate with the right to privacy?
cards.a: The right 'to be let alone' (also phrased 'to be left alone')-a reaction to intrusive new media such as press photography.

figure.alt: Warren and Brandeis privacy history slide
figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What does Article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) protect regarding privacy?
cards.a: No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks upon honour and reputation; everyone has the right to legal protection against such interference or attacks.

cards.q: How does Westin (1967) define privacy (as cited in the course intro)?
cards.a: The claim of individuals to determine for themselves when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: In Lecture 1's fairness framing, how are costs/risks of data use asymmetric between controller and individual?
cards.a: Controllers gain from collection/use (income, control, expertise) while individuals bear inspection costs, breach/abuse harms (reputation, loss, threats), knowledge asymmetry, and reduced freedom/control-access to personal data creates power over people.

figure.alt: Duality of risks diagram from Canvas
figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is the 'chilling effect' in the society/privacy slides?
cards.a: People retreat from controversial matters and relationships when institutions/controllers exercise power via data-undermining trust and participation.

figure.caption: Behaviour changes under watch
figure.shows: Behaviour changes under watch

cards.q: Name core basic privacy principles from OECD Guidelines / Lecture 1.
cards.a: Lawfulness (e.g. informed consent / collection limitation); data minimisation & avoidance; purpose specification & purpose binding (use limitation); transparency & intervenability; appropriate security; accountability. Note: 'non-sensitive' data do not exist-function creep examples include loyalty-card misuse and Lidl video monitoring.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is 'function creep' (purpose misuse) as taught in Lecture 1?
cards.a: Using data collected for one purpose for another, unintended purpose-e.g. loyalty-card data against customer interests, or workplace video monitoring scandals (Lidl 2006).

figure.alt: Stated purpose drifting to new uses
figure.caption: Purpose limitation risk
figure.shows: Purpose limitation risk

cards.q: What privacy milestone followed the Bismarck deathbed photo scandal (1898)?
cards.a: Photographers entered the bedroom, staged the corpse for photos, and offered copies via newspaper ads; they were arrested and imprisoned. In 1907 a law on the 'right on own image' followed (Lecture 1 history).

cards.q: Name three 'obvious use cases' for privacy from Lecture 1 (how privacy shapes society).
cards.a: Voting secrecy as a foundation for democracy; protection against discrimination based on political opinion, relationships, religion or philosophy; enabling personal freedom and independence in thinking and development. Access to and control over personal data creates power over individuals.

cards.q: What is the asymmetric cost problem in Lecture 1's fairness framing?
cards.a: Data controllers can collect and use data relatively easily, while the individual bears the hard work of inspecting and stopping collection/use.

cards.q: What is the asymmetric knowledge problem between controller and individual (Lecture 1)?
cards.a: Controllers have domain experts, budgets, and knowledge of business models and data processing/informatics; individuals typically do not.

cards.q: How does Lecture 1 frame profit asymmetry around personal data?
cards.a: Controllers get income and growth from data (and 'free' apps); individuals face price discrimination, impulse shopping pressure, and being judged by others.

cards.q: What 'attack on sovereignty' risk does Lecture 1 link to data about members of society?
cards.a: Knowledge about each member enables selecting, discriminating and manipulating public discourse, public trust and public reputation; individuals need transparency about origins and motivation of communication.

cards.q: How does GDPR relate to Norwegian law in Lecture 1's privacy-principles overview?
cards.a: In EU/EFTA, GDPR is 'translated' into national laws-e.g. Personopplysningsloven in Norway. Historically: national laws from the 1970s, then EU harmonisation via a directive, then GDPR (with e-Privacy enrichment still expected); other regions and sectors (health, finance) have their own rules.

cards.q: What does Lecture 1 claim about so-called 'non-sensitive' data?
cards.a: 'Non-sensitive' data do not exist: purpose misuse / function creep can turn ordinary data into harmful uses (examples: Lidl video monitoring; loyalty-card data used against customer interests).

figure.alt: Ordinary data reused for new purposes
figure.caption: Function creep undermines 'non-sensitive' labels
figure.shows: Purpose binding matters even for everyday data.

cards.q: Which public tracker does Lecture 1 Case study 1 point to for real GDPR fines?
cards.a: The GDPR fines / enforcement tracker at enforcementtracker.com-use it to pick an organisation, understand its business motive, identify which GDPR part was violated, and summarise for class.

cards.q: What tool does Lecture 1 Case study 2 recommend for checking legal grounds for processing?
cards.a: The ICO lawful-basis interactive guidance tool (ico.org.uk GDPR resources): pick a site with a clear service and privacy policy, then evaluate legal grounds for processing.

cards.q: What does Lecture 1 Case study 3 use Webbkoll (webbkoll.dataskydd.net) for?
cards.a: Assess third-party data sharing on a chosen web page: compare the privacy policy's sharing claims with what Webbkoll observes in practice, then summarise findings.

cards.q: What does Lecture 1 say data minimisation and avoidance require (OECD-linked)?
cards.a: Data should be adequate, relevant and not excessive; minimise collection, use, sharing, linkability and retention (cf. OECD Data Quality / related principles).

cards.q: What is the asymmetric control / power problem in Lecture 1's fairness framing?
cards.a: Controllers gain control and power through access to personal data, while individuals lose freedom and practical control over how data about them is used-data access becomes power over people.

cards.q: What do purpose specification and purpose binding require (OECD / Lecture 1 basic principles)?
cards.a: Collect and process data only for specified, explicit purposes (purpose specification); do not reuse for incompatible purposes (purpose binding / use limitation). Function creep violates this.

cards.q: Why is the CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability) insufficient for data protection / privacy?
cards.a: CIA secures systems and data against unauthorised access, tampering and downtime, but does not cover privacy-specific goals such as transparency, intervenability and unlinkability (or purpose limitation / fairness). Data protection needs CIA plus those privacy protection goals.

figure.alt: CIA triad alone is not full data protection
figure.caption: CIA is necessary but not sufficient for privacy
figure.shows: Add transparency, intervenability, unlinkability (SDM / Hansen et al.).

cards.q: How is ACIT4280 taught (format) according to the Aug 13 2026 intro?
cards.a: Flipped classroom: students read/watch Canvas material before class; bi-weekly online lectures with case studies & student presentations; group home assignment (groups of 3) with written report + presentation; final timed digital exam on Inspera.

cards.q: What does Art. 12 require for communicating with data subjects?
cards.a: Information must be concise, transparent, intelligible, easily accessible, in clear and plain language (Art. 29 WP recommends multi-layered privacy policies). Prefer electronic means for electronic requests; may use standardised machine-readable icons.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What key information must transparency/access cover (Art. 13 & 15)?
cards.a: Controller identity & contact (incl. DPO); purposes & legal basis; recipients; international transfers; retention periods; data subject rights; existence of automated decision-making (logic, significance, consequences). Access: electronic copy of the data (Art. 15), without adversely affecting others' rights/freedoms (trade secrets, IP).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: When does the right to erasure (Art. 17) apply?
cards.a: Without undue delay when data are no longer necessary; consent withdrawn and no other legal basis; objection succeeds; unlawful processing; legal obligation to erase; and related grounds in Art. 17. If made public, take reasonable steps to inform other controllers.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is the right to data portability (Art. 20), and what does it exclude?
cards.a: Where processing is based on consent or contract: receive personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and transmit to another controller (or have it transmitted directly). Does not include derived data or data received from third parties (e.g. reputation scores).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What do Art. 21 and Art. 22 protect?
cards.a: Art. 21: right to object to processing based on legitimate interests/public interest (incl. profiling), to direct marketing (incl. profiling), and in some research/statistics cases. Art. 22: right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects the person.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Why is Google Spain / Costeja (C-131/12) linked to data subject rights in the materials?
cards.a: CJEU judgment on the 'right to be forgotten' / delisting-connected in course materials to erasure/transparency rights (Art. 17 context).

figure.alt: Search results and right to be forgotten
figure.caption: Costeja balancing
figure.shows: Costeja balancing

cards.q: What 'clear rules for business' does the L8 GDPR obligations material highlight?
cards.a: One single set of rules; one-stop-shop (deal with one lead supervisory authority); European rules on European soil (non-EU companies offering services in the EU must apply the same rules); risk-based approach.

figure.caption: One-stop-shop idea
figure.shows: One-stop-shop idea

cards.q: What are the GDPR data-breach notification duties (Art. 33-34)?
cards.a: Notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours (Art. 33). Notify the data subject if the breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms (Art. 34).

figure.caption: Art. 33 clock
figure.shows: Art. 33 clock

cards.q: What does security of processing (Art. 32) emphasise?
cards.a: Appropriate technical and organisational measures ensuring confidentiality, integrity and availability-examples include pseudonymisation and/or encryption.

figure.caption: Art. 32 includes encryption as a security measure
figure.shows: Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext.

cards.q: What are Art. 30 records and Art. 38 DPO obligations (high level)?
cards.a: Controllers/processors must maintain records of processing activities (Art. 30). Designate a DPO (Art. 38) unless processing is not a core business activity (as framed in L8 slides).

cards.q: How may personal data be transferred to third countries (Art. 45-49 overview)?
cards.a: Primarily where the Commission has decided an adequate level of protection (Art. 45). Otherwise safeguards such as standard contractual clauses (Art. 46), binding corporate rules (Art. 47), or limited exceptions (Art. 49, e.g. explicit consent). Materials note Privacy Shield replaced Safe Harbor after Schrems, with ongoing adequacy concerns.

figure.caption: Art. 45-49 overview
figure.shows: Art. 45-49 overview

cards.q: What is the two-tier administrative fine structure under Art. 83?
cards.a: Lower tier: up to the greater of EUR10 million or 2% of global annual turnover. Higher tier (serious breaches): up to the greater of EUR20 million or 4% of global annual turnover. Fines must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

figure.caption: Art. 83 percentages
figure.shows: Art. 83 percentages

cards.q: What replaced the Article 29 Working Party under the GDPR institutional setup?
cards.a: The European Data Protection Board (EDPB), Art. 68-73. Supervisory authorities (Art. 51-59) monitor, assess and enforce; data subjects can lodge complaints.

figure.caption: Institutional continuity
figure.shows: Institutional continuity

cards.q: How does the draft ePrivacy Regulation relate to the GDPR?
cards.a: It is lex specialis to the GDPR: specific privacy rules for electronic communications; intended as a directly applicable Regulation replacing the ePrivacy ('Cookie') Directive; extends to OTT services such as Skype, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, Gmail, etc.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Name proposed main rules of the draft ePrivacy Regulation (L9).
cards.a: Privacy rules for communication content & metadata; simpler cookie rules (no consent for non-privacy-intrusive cookies; privacy-friendly browser defaults); anti-spam protection; limited processing by traditional telecoms for additional services/business development; enforcement by DPAs also in charge under GDPR.

figure.caption: Communications focus
figure.shows: Communications focus

cards.q: What 'grave' concerns did Art. 29 WP raise about the draft ePrivacy Regulation?
cards.a: Tracking of terminal equipment location; conditions for analysing content & metadata; tracking walls; default settings of terminal equipment/software.

figure.alt: ePrivacy draft concerns relative to GDPR
figure.caption: WP29 critique context
figure.shows: WP29 critique context

cards.q: Give PET examples mapped to data minimisation (L10).
cards.a: Anonymity/pseudonymity tools: communication-level (Mixes, DC-nets, Tor, steganography); application-level (anonymous credentials, anonymous payment, PIR); data-level (k-anonymity, differential privacy, secret sharing).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1 / L10). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1 / L10). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Which PETs/tools are mapped to purpose limitation in L10?
cards.a: Privacy policy languages, sticky policies, functional separation.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1 / L10). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1 / L10). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Which approaches map to lawfulness/fairness/transparency in L10?
cards.a: Algorithmic transparency & ethical data management, Fairness by Design, ex ante and ex post Transparency Enhancing Tools (TETs).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1 / L10). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1 / L10). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Which controls map to integrity & confidentiality (Art. 5) in L10?
cards.a: Security controls including access control, authentication, encryption (e.g. TLS), logging.

figure.caption: Security PETs include encryption and access control
figure.shows: Padlock = confidentiality control.

cards.q: What maps to accountability in the L10 GDPR->PETs mapping?
cards.a: Privacy-preserving transparency logging, provenance, consent management.

figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 1 / L10). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is the ACIT4280 exam format (saved course plan FALL 2026)?
cards.a: Individual digital written exam, 3 hours, no aids (A-F). Coursework: one group assignment (report + presentation).

cards.q: What has PET research historically focused on (Lecture 2)?
cards.a: Information hiding and control, inspired by legal/human-rights perspectives-yet there is a noted lack of widely deployed PETs in the 'real world'.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Name key PET concepts to remember from Pfitzmann-Hansen (Lecture 2).
cards.a: Unobservability; anonymity & pseudonymity; partial identities; unlinkability.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: In basic identity-based transactions, what is the difference between identification, authentication, and authorization?
cards.a: Identification: who is the user. Authentication: prove it is really that user. Authorization/non-repudiation: permit actions/documents (often with digital signatures) and create receipts. Pseudonyms can support privacy-enhancing identity management.

figure.caption: Identity transaction basics
figure.shows: Identity transaction basics

cards.q: What are 'synthetic identities' in Lecture 2?
cards.a: Identifiers created from observed data (IP, combined accounts/location, behavioural mining, biometrics) beyond the data subject's control-can become person-related (e.g. via home/work patterns in location tracks).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is the Anonymity Trilemma (Lecture 2)?
cards.a: Strong anonymity, low bandwidth, and low latency-choose two (Das et al.). Tor is framed as a low-latency anonymity network (relays/bridges) for anonymous browsing.

figure.caption: Anonymity trilemma and Tor trade-offs
figure.shows: Onion layers hide who talks to whom.

cards.q: How does Lecture 3 distinguish privacy from data protection?
cards.a: Privacy is fuzzy, contextual, a social construct. Data protection must be more discrete; proportionality of processing is key. Data protection is necessary but not sufficient for privacy.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: List Ann Cavoukian's seven Privacy by Design principles (Lecture 3).
cards.a: 1) Proactive not reactive / preventative not remedial; 2) Privacy as the default; 3) Privacy embedded into design; 4) Full functionality-positive-sum, not zero-sum; 5) End-to-end security-full lifecycle protection; 6) Visibility and transparency-keep it open; 7) Respect for user privacy-keep it user-centric.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Which privacy protection goals complement CIA in the Standard Data Protection Model / Hansen et al. (Lecture 3)?
cards.a: Alongside confidentiality (and CIA): transparency, intervenability, and unlinkability (privacy goals from the German DP community / SDM). Summary slide also frames CIA + unlinkability + transparency + intervenability.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Name the three privacy research paradigms in Lecture 3.
cards.a: Privacy as Confidentiality; Privacy as Control; Privacy as Practice.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What practical limit of Cavoukian's PbD principles does Lecture 3 stress for developers?
cards.a: The seven principles do not provide hands-on instructions for engineers-you must still ask how to implement each principle in software.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) according to Lecture 4?
cards.a: A systematic process for identifying and evaluating privacy risks/impacts of a project. Anticipatory-done in advance or in parallel with the initiative-not only a one-off report.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: How does qualitative risk assessment combine impact and likelihood (Lecture 4)?
cards.a: Risk(A) ~ impact(T(A)) x likelihood(T(A)) for threat T on asset A; classify resulting levels (typically low/moderate/high). Consider significance, likelihood, and magnitude of impact.

figure.alt: Risk chart from Canvas course files
figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What outcomes are expected from a PIA (Lecture 4 summary)?
cards.a: Identify privacy impacts; assess them from all stakeholders' perspectives; show how negative impacts can be avoided or lessened; clarify residual/accepted impacts where unavoidable.

figure.alt: PIA table from Canvas course files
figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What bias in privacy risk assessment does Lecture 4 warn about?
cards.a: Risk management often focuses on risks to service providers/system owners rather than end users-yet all stakeholders are threatened; long-term privacy risk models (incl. duality of risks) are lacking.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Why is IT security management described as a 'horizontal' activity (Lecture 5)?
cards.a: It cuts across quality, operations, HR, and facility management-most departments contact security management. Organizing an ISMS needs management support, a cross-role panel, and regular incident/priority meetings.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is risk treatment via controls (Lecture 5)?
cards.a: Select and implement technical and/or administrative controls (from catalogues such as ISO 27001 annex / NIST SP 800-53 privacy & security controls) to reduce or remove risks in infrastructure, procedures and resources.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Outline the incident-management stages from ISO/IEC 27035 as taught in Lecture 5.
cards.a: 1) Plan and prepare (policy, IR/CSIRT team); 2) Detect and report; 3) Assess/decide it is an incident; 4) Respond (contain, eradicate, recover, forensics); 5) Lessons learned / improvements.

figure.caption: ISO/IEC 27035 sketch
figure.shows: ISO/IEC 27035 sketch

cards.q: What does Lecture 5 emphasise about many privacy controls?
cards.a: Many privacy controls are administrative (not only technical). Privacy/security management is a complex multi-role process; prepare relationships with emergency response before incidents happen.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is an e-ID in Lecture 2 terms?
cards.a: A portion of digital data plus algorithms (hard/software) whose purpose is to convince a computer that a particular, possibly privileged, person is using it - may be official (passport-based) or soft (email/pseudonym).

figure.caption: Digital identity evidence
figure.shows: Digital identity evidence

cards.q: Name Pfitzmann-style categories of identity control from Lecture 2.
cards.a: Me-Identity (what I define), Our-Identity (what others and I define), Their-Identity (what others define as my identity).

figure.caption: Who defines identity
figure.shows: Who defines identity

cards.q: What is identifiability (Pfitzmann-Hansen) as taught in Lecture 2?
cards.a: From an attacker's view: the attacker can sufficiently identify the subject within an identifiability set - subjects may be indistinguishable or distinguishable by attributes/usage patterns.

figure.caption: Pfitzmann-Hansen
figure.shows: Pfitzmann-Hansen

cards.q: Beyond CIA, which AAA security objectives does Lecture 2 list?
cards.a: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (logging/tracking of users and data/sessions).

figure.caption: AAA beside CIA
figure.shows: AAA beside CIA

cards.q: What classic paper/idea starts mix networks in Lecture 2?
cards.a: David Chaum (1981) "Untraceable Electronic Mail, Return Addresses, and Digital Pseudonyms" - mix format and mixing strategy for strong anonymity (often at latency/bandwidth cost).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is a typical Tor circuit path for anonymous browsing (Lecture 2)?
cards.a: Client traffic goes via guard (entry), middle, and exit relays - low-latency anonymity network for browsing; bridges help when Tor is blocked.

figure.caption: Tor path through relays
figure.shows: Entry, middle and exit hops peel layers.

cards.q: What anonymity property do onion services emphasise (Lecture 2)?
cards.a: Recipient anonymity (who is receiving requests) plus self-authenticated, end-to-end encrypted services; single onion services are a related deployment variant.

figure.caption: Onion routing principle
figure.shows: Layers of encryption like an onion.

cards.q: Ex-ante vs ex-post Transparency Enhancing Tools (TETs) - give examples from Lecture 2.
cards.a: Ex-ante: privacy policy languages (e.g. P3P/PPL), multi-layered policies and icons. Ex-post: dashboards / Data Track-style tools that show what was disclosed and support access/intervenability.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Lecture 2 summary: privacy protection consists of which elements?
cards.a: Protect communication content and relationship; protect identities; conceal activity (unobservability); unlinkability of actions; transparency of collection/processing/storage; intervenability and rectification opportunities.

figure.caption: Lecture 2 wrap-up
figure.shows: Lecture 2 wrap-up

cards.q: What objectives do PETs target beyond raw data security (Lecture 2)?
cards.a: Control over personal data / transparency; data minimisation/avoidance; identity management; lawful processing; plus data security and integrity.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 2). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What "trilogy" of applications does Cavoukian's PbD extend to (Lecture 3)?
cards.a: 1) IT systems; 2) accountable business practices; 3) physical design and networked infrastructure.

figure.caption: Systems practices infrastructure
figure.shows: Systems practices infrastructure

cards.q: What does "Privacy as the Default" mean (Cavoukian principle 2)?
cards.a: Maximum privacy without user action - personal data are automatically protected; if the individual does nothing, privacy remains intact.

figure.alt: Data protection by design and by default
figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What does Cavoukian's "positive-sum, not zero-sum" principle argue?
cards.a: Accommodate legitimate interests in a win-win way - avoid false dichotomies such as privacy vs security; both can be designed together.

figure.caption: Not privacy versus security
figure.shows: Not privacy versus security

cards.q: Give example measures for unlinkability (Standard Data Protection Model / Lecture 3).
cards.a: Restrict processing/transfer rights; close unnecessary interfaces; organisational separation; purpose-specific pseudonyms/anonymisation/anonymous credentials; regulated purpose-change procedures.

figure.caption: Separate and pseudonymise
figure.shows: Separate and pseudonymise

cards.q: What does intervenability require in practice (Lecture 3)?
cards.a: Means for consent/withdrawal/objection; support for rights (correct/block/erase); SPoC for data subjects; traceability of controller actions granting rights - ability to intervene in processing.

figure.caption: Act on processing
figure.shows: Act on processing

cards.q: What characterises the "Privacy as Confidentiality" research paradigm?
cards.a: Once data is disclosed, privacy is lost; emphasis on data minimisation and crypto; centralised collection seen as bad; strong open-source/reproducibility culture.

figure.caption: Hide and minimise
figure.shows: Hide and minimise

cards.q: What characterises "Privacy as Control"?
cards.a: Privacy as ability to control personal data - purpose, intervenability, transparency, accountability (classic data-protection framing); disclosure may still be in your interest (e.g. healthcare).

figure.caption: Data protection framing
figure.shows: Data protection framing

cards.q: Hansen mistake 1: what is "Storage as Default"?
cards.a: Storing personal data without justifying need, retention period, and access control - violates minimisation, purpose binding, and right to be forgotten.

figure.caption: Justify retention
figure.shows: Justify retention

cards.q: Hansen mistake 2: what is "Linkability as Default"?
cards.a: No unidentified use possible; transactions are linkable across contexts - enables profiling and may violate minimisation/purpose binding.

figure.caption: Prefer unlinkable use
figure.shows: Prefer unlinkable use

cards.q: PIA vs DPIA mandatory status as stressed in Lecture 3?
cards.a: PIAs are not generally mandatory; DPIAs are required only in particular high-risk cases (GDPR Art. 35). Treating every PIA as mandatory can cause "PIA fatigue".

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Why is treating PIA as a one-time early task a mistake (Lecture 3)?
cards.a: PIA should be a continuing process across the lifecycle, not a single checklist completed once and forgotten for years.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 3). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: How does Lecture 3 separate cause and effect in privacy risk layers?
cards.a: Cause: user privacy risks / infringement of personal life. Effects for the organisation: reputation damage, fines, lawsuits, loss of trust. Do not only manage organisational effects.

figure.alt: User privacy risk versus org effects
figure.caption: Cause versus effect
figure.shows: Cause versus effect

cards.q: Which four privacy targets should a PIA consider (Lecture 4 summary)?
cards.a: Privacy of personal information; privacy of the person; privacy of personal behaviour; privacy of personal communications.

figure.caption: Broader than data fields
figure.shows: Broader than data fields

cards.q: Name several core PIA elements from PIAF (Lecture 4).
cards.a: Ongoing process; scalability; all privacy types; accountability; transparency; stakeholder involvement; publication/registry (with sensitive-info limits); risk management and legal compliance; audit and review.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Preventive vs detective, technical vs non-technical controls (Lecture 4)?
cards.a: Preventive: stop violations; detective: detect them. Technical: PETs/security in the system. Non-technical: processes, procedures, policies, operations.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: How does Solove's taxonomy help PIA impact thinking (readings/Lecture 4)?
cards.a: Privacy-violating actions: information collection, processing, dissemination, and invasions - risk starts already at collection, before invasion.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What ENISA SME impact levels are taught for individuals' privacy harm?
cards.a: Low (minor inconvenience), Medium (significant but manageable inconvenience), High (serious difficulties), Very high (significant/irreversible consequences).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What should a PIA report typically contain (Lecture 4)?
cards.a: Project description; privacy issues analysis; business case for any intrusion; alternatives considered; privacy design features; residual risks; recommendations and implementation/audit path.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 4). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What continuous cycle frames ISO/security management in Lecture 5?
cards.a: Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA): continuous improvement over repeated rounds of planning, implementing controls, monitoring, and corrective action.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Give examples of ISO/IEC 27001:2013 Annex A domains from Lecture 5.
cards.a: Among 14 domains: policies; organisation; HR security; asset management; access control; cryptography; physical security; operations; communications; system acquisition/dev; suppliers; incident management; business continuity; compliance.

figure.caption: Annex A overview
figure.shows: Annex A overview

cards.q: List triggers that should start a new PDCA / re-assessment (Lecture 5).
cards.a: Regular schedule; infrastructure/software/supplier/outsourcing changes; major updates; staff/location/product changes; "world change" (new attacks, tools, crypto breaks).

figure.caption: When to re-run PDCA
figure.shows: When to re-run PDCA

cards.q: What do the LINDDUN letters stand for (Lecture 5/6)?
cards.a: Linkability, Identifiability, Non-repudiation, Detectability, Disclosure of information, Unawareness, Non-compliance - privacy threat categories used with DFDs/threat trees.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 5). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Who are typical ISMS "players" vs subjects in Lecture 5?
cards.a: Players: Board, CEO, ISMS Forum (CTO/CSO/DPO/management/product owners). Subjects: humans and assets (equipment, networks, apps, information stores).

figure.caption: Governance roles
figure.shows: Governance roles

cards.q: What risk-analysis task does the smart-car factory case ask groups to do?
cards.a: Identify critical information assets; find security/privacy threats per asset; assess likelihood/damage (ENISA-style); rank risks highest to lowest - applying management method to a connected production scenario.

figure.caption: Assets threats ranking
figure.shows: Assets threats ranking

cards.q: How is OASIS Privacy by Design for Software Engineers framed in Lecture 5?
cards.a: As a PDCA-style method that includes risk analysis - privacy management documentation approach for engineers (PbD-SE).

cards.q: List Hoepman-style privacy design strategies from Lecture 6.
cards.a: Minimise; Hide; Separate; Aggregate (abstract); Inform; Control; Enforce; Demonstrate.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What does the Minimise strategy ask (Lecture 6)?
cards.a: Restrict personal data processed to the minimal amount needed for the purpose; ask if another design fulfils the purpose with less data (e.g. pseudonyms instead of real names).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What does the Separate strategy recommend?
cards.a: Process personal data in distributed compartments when possible - prefer distributed/local over centralised remote processing (e.g. contact data and purchase data in separate stores).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Why is Demonstrate especially GDPR-relevant (Lecture 6)?
cards.a: Controllers must be able to show how the privacy policy and legal requirements are implemented (accountability) - e.g. recent audit evidence.

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: Name privacy dark patterns from the Lecture 6 survey excerpt.
cards.a: Privacy Zuckering; Bad Defaults; Forced Registration; Hidden Legalese; Immortal Accounts; Address Book Leeching; Shadow User Profiles (several tied to identity management).

figure.caption: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.
figure.shows: From course materials (ACIT4280 Lecture 6). Source: lecture slides / Canvas.

cards.q: What is the dark pattern "Fogging identification with security"?
cards.a: While collecting identity attributes, the service claims the extra data is for the user's security - obscuring the real acquisition purpose (MAXIMIZE/CENTRALIZE/OBSCURE strategies).

figure.caption: Purpose obscured
figure.shows: Purpose obscured

cards.q: How does Lecture 6 summarise software architecture (IEEE 1471-style)?
cards.a: Fundamental organisation of a system: components, relationships to each other and the environment, and principles guiding design and evolution.

cards.q: Name top-level ISO 25010 quality attributes listed in Lecture 6 (incl. security).
cards.a: Functional suitability; performance efficiency; compatibility; usability; reliability; security; maintainability; portability.

figure.caption: ISO 25010 includes security
figure.shows: ISO 25010 includes security

cards.q: What lecture themes does ACIT4280 cover after the GDPR foundations?
cards.a: PETs (L2); Privacy by Design / protection goals / paradigms (L3); PIA and privacy risk (L4); privacy/security management and cases (L5); privacy engineering, strategies, patterns and dark patterns (L6).
